source.title: Neural Scaling Laws Rooted in the Data Distribution

record.tranche_reason: The study tests scaling behavior in toy percolation regression experiments, using mean squared error rather than language-model pretraining cross-entropy and a different model and dataset setup.
record.gate_note: The paper's reported Chinchilla exponents and other empirical results from cited work are not this study's results. The paper's own scaling experiments and its test of the proposed DOF allocation are recorded below.
record.test_reason: This is a theory paper explaining why scaling laws exist via a percolation model of data. Its only experiments use a Bayesian nearest-neighbor regressor, not a neural network, on synthetic percolation-cluster data with MSE loss. They check the theory's own predicted curves and DOF allocation. They do not measure language-model loss scaling (V1–V4, V6, V7) or neural models in other modalities or regimes (V5). The comparison with Chinchilla exponents uses cited results (Hoffmann et al.; Besiroglu et al.), not new measurements. The dmodel∝P^0.387 fit in Appendix L concerns architecture hyperparameters, not loss.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is largely correct. The authors propose that percolation structure in data yields two scaling regimes, quanta (subcritical) and manifold approximation (supercritical), unifying prior theories. Toy regression experiments match predictions. They also compare predicted exponents to Chinchilla's reported ones: model exponent 1 or 0.387 depending on the DOF-to-parameter conversion; data exponent 0.5 versus the observed 0.28–0.37. They suggest more efficient LLM data scaling may be possible.
record.recipe_differences: The study derives scaling predictions from a percolation model and tests them with nearest-neighbor regression on synthetic datasets using mean squared error; it does not reproduce language-model scaling experiments using pretraining cross-entropy.
record.method_sensitivity: The theory predicts different scaling regimes depending on percolation criticality and the ratio c/D relative to the cluster-distribution exponent; experiments use criticality and c = 2.

fits_no_version.finding: A Bayesian nearest-neighbor regressor on critical Bethe-lattice percolation data shows model and data scaling curves that match the theory's no-free-parameter predictions (Fig. 6). Individual clusters scale with exponent c/D=0.5 (Fig. 8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Power-law scaling of a non-neural toy approximator on percolation-structured synthetic data follows the percolation theory's predicted curves.

fits_no_version.finding: The best tested DOF allocations among clusters (2000 random b, kbr combinations at N=250, 500, 1000) appear consistent with the theoretically optimal allocation (Eq. 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the toy setup, the loss-minimizing allocation of capacity across power-law-sized subtasks matches the theory's predicted allocation.

record.problems: Evidence comes from synthetic percolation regression with a nearest-neighbor model and mean squared error, not language-model pretraining. The scaling experiments use the critical regime and c = 2. Results are shown in figures rather than given as numerical scaling-curve values in the text.

untested.parts: All: no language-model pretraining loss measured.
All: no extrapolation from small to large runs.
All: no compute-optimal parameter/token split measured. Chinchilla exponents are only cited.
All: no neural models in other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer. The toy experiments use a nearest-neighbor regressor.
All: downstream tasks are only discussed qualitatively (App. K).
All: the DOF-to-parameter conversion issue is raised theoretically (App. C) but no fits are compared.

record.verdict_notes: The reader labelled this study tests/T2 with a V5 'supports' verdict. That is rejected: the experimental system is a non-neural nearest-neighbor regressor on synthetic data built to test the paper's own theory, so it does not bear on any claim version. The Chinchilla numbers in Sec. 6.1 are cited, not measured.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining cross-entropy scaling against parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small runs predict substantially larger runs.
The compute-optimal split between language-model parameters and training tokens, and how either grows with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Image and video models, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, and transfer; the experiments use synthetic regression datasets only.
Downstream-task performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of empirically fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits on fitting choices, and systematic departures of empirical curves from a single power law.

rows.subject: nearest-neighbor regression model
rows.operation_detail: Measured loss as training degrees of freedom increased, using the theoretically specified DOF allocation for model scaling.

conditions.value: percolation clusters on a Bethe lattice at criticality; d = 100

rows.measure: Test loss versus training degrees of freedom (model scaling).
rows.uncertainty: 1 standard deviation error bars; plotted points are medians with 16th and 84th percentiles.
rows.note: The text says the results match the theoretical predictions well. The plotted outcome is not reported as a numeric value in the text.
rows.check: The subject is a nearest-neighbor regressor on synthetic percolation data, not a neural model in another modality or training regime. It is a different kind of system than V5 names. The row shows the study's own theory matching its toy experiment (Fig. 6a), so it should not be linked to V5.

conditions.value: percolation clusters on a Bethe lattice at criticality; d = 100

rows.uncertainty: 1 standard deviation error bars; plotted points are medians with 16th and 84th percentiles.

rows.check: Same issue as r1: this is data scaling of a non-neural toy approximator against the paper's own prediction (Fig. 6b). It does not bear on V5.

rows.subject: function approximator with parameterized DOF distribution

rows.note: The text says the best parameters appear consistent with the theoretically optimal ones. This tests allocation of DOF among clusters, not the parameter-and-token split in V3.
